utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, ladies and gentlemen; good morning, interpreters. Can you hear me? Yes. I think they hear. I can hear them as well. Good morning, technicians; good morning, court reporters, legal officers, whom we often forget; good morning, counsel for the Prosecution; good morning, counsel for the Defence; good morning, General Krstic; good morning, everyone. I owe you an explanation. Yesterday I told you that the hearing would be held in Courtroom II. I know that the technicians have been working all night so that we could be here this morning, but these frequent changes add up to the stress that we already have to deal with due to the nature of our work. All other stresses should be, therefore, avoided. At any rate, let me present my apologies to you and the public in general. The intention was to enable us to work in the best possible conditions. Be that as it may, Mr. Harmon, could you tell us what is the situation with witnesses this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Good morning, and good morning to my colleagues. We have a witness we're going to proceed with. Mr. McCloskey will lead the evidence of that witness. Before we begin, however, I'd like to just clarify one matter for the Court and for the record. Yesterday, through Corporal Van der Zwan, I introduced a patch. It's Prosecutor's Exhibit 93. He said he got it when he was at OP Uniform from a Bosnian Serb soldiers. So the record is perfectly clear, the letters at the top which are in Cyrillic say "Bratunac", the letters in Cyrillic underneath the image say "brigade," and underneath brigade in Cyrillic are written the letters "VRS," and my colleagues from the Defence have looked at this exhibit and they agree with me that that is what this represents. I wanted to clarify the record so it would be clear. Now, without further ado, Mr. McCloskey will introduce the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Harmon, before we proceed, let me ask you one other question. Exhibit 32C, Prosecutor's 32C, the French translation is not complete, and we had 25 minutes of transcript, at least. I don't know whether you have a complete version or is this just a sample of the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Unfortunately, it's not a sample. It's the official transcript of the Tribunal from the hearing that we took from -- it's the final transcription. I didn't know it was missing 25 minutes until one of the interpreters kindly informed me at the conclusion of the hearing that it was missing 25 minutes. So we merely introduced the official transcript. We will now -- we now find it's missing 25 minutes. We will endeavour to get those 25 minutes translated and we'll submit that at a later date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. As I told you, Mr. Harmon, I shared your view. At the same time, I was happy, but also a bit disappointed, because when this comes to a French translation, it seems that we always have problems. So, Mr. Harmon, you will prepare a complete version for us, and then afterwards it will be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Thank you for your attention. Mr. McCloskey, I believe, is going to take the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. The next witness is a protected witness, and we've discussed that with the Defence. He asked for face distortion and pseudonym, so I see we're set up for it. But, of course, we still need the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Petrusic, do you have any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the record, Mr. President, the Defence has no objections whatsoever regarding the issue mentioned by Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Petrusic. Mr. Usher or Mr. Registrar, can you please lower down the blinds. After five minutes, we will put them up again, after the witness has been brought into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dubuisson, the usher has not gone to Bosnia to fetch the witness, I hope. Oh. He's coming.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you hear me, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. Sir, we will call you Witness I, for your protection, because you have asked for certain protective measures which have been accorded to you. So you will be referred to as Witness I. First of all, could you please read the solemn declaration that the usher will give you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may be seated now. Witness I, could you please have a look at this piece of paper that the registrar will show you, and could you please confirm if the name written on it is your name or not? Could you please answer simply by saying yes or no.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well then. So on this piece of paper it was your name that was written. Are you comfortable, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should first like to thank you, Witness I, for coming to the Tribunal. Let me just explain to you that you will first answer questions that will be put to you by Mr. McCloskey, whom you probably already know. Mr. McCloskey, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness I. How are you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Good morning. Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. I'll be asking you a few questions like the President said, and if you can just do your best to answer, and you may notice that I interrupt you occasionally, and we'll eventually be able to get through your story. Okay?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you first tell us where you were born?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: I was born in the Srebrenica municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what is your birth date?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: 18th of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Of what year?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: (redacted).

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where did you spend most of your life?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Most of my life I spent in Srebrenica. I would venture outside Srebrenica a little bit because of my work.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what was your work?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: I was a farmer. I also work a little bit as a bricklayer and had some other small jobs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And in July of 1995, where were you living?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: I was living in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And on July 11th of 1995, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: It was at that time that Srebrenica fell, and I went down to Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you take family members of yours with you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes, I did, my family.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you tell us -- can you describe which family members you went with to Potocari?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: My wife was with me, my daughter. I had four grandchildren and a daughter-in-law.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Roughly, how old were your grandchildren at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Well, the youngest one, who had just been born, was very small. He was born as soon as the war began.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how about the oldest one? About how old was that grandchild?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Well, the oldest one is now in the seventh grade of the elementary school, so he's 14 now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And did you have two sons at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes, I did. They had gone through the woods.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And have you seen them since that time that they went through the woods?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: No, I haven't. I just know that the youngest one went to the hospital, took out all the wounded persons to UNPROFOR, put them on a truck, and then afterwards he left and went through the woods.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you find that out by one of the wounded people that he helped?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes, from one of the wounded people I learned about that. He later on came to Batkovic. And there were many others who remained, who did not arrive, but they had been registered prior to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So that first night in Potocari, did you spend the night outside one of the factories with your family?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I was within the compound, but I couldn't actually get inside the factory. They were crowded. There were several factories there, and I was actually outside in the area surrounding the factory, not far from the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So was that first night July 11th?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes, it was, the first night.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, on July 12th, can you tell us what happened on July 12th, as you recall it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: On the 12th of July, a man came with a kind of trumpet and started talking to us. He told us that there had been some negotiations, that we should not be afraid, that the Serb soldiers would now come and mix with the people and so that they would see if there were any weapons there, but, anyhow, that nobody should be afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what happened after that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: After that, they came to us and they kept walking around amongst the people until the afternoon that day. At one point they started taking people, one by one, away.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When you say "they," who are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Serb soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where did you spend that night of the 12th?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: I spent it outside in the open, also in Potocari. And on that day, they brought some bread in a little TAM truck. He also distributed some sweets and recorded everything with a camera. They wanted to show the world how humane they were, whereas while they were committing genocide, they were not filming anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So again when you say "they," you're talking about Serb soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Serb soldiers. They were filming while they were throwing bread onto the people and distributing sweets, and there was a presenter there who was filming everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So were you present in the crowd and saw the Serb soldiers doing this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes. I saw it and I managed to catch a loaf of bread, because in Srebrenica, I had nothing to take with me, so I wanted to give this food to my grandchildren so they could eat something. I saw everything with my own eyes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What else did you see that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: I saw a number of dogs, maybe eight or nine, German Shepherds, walking around with soldiers amongst the people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: They were taking some men away, saying that they wanted to have a chat with them. Maybe they were their neighbours. I don't know. So they kept walking around a little bit, and they took them away. But in the evening, they started taking people away in greater numbers. At one point, people started to scream, and everybody stood up. Afterwards, we heard rumours that a woman had given birth. And then after a few minutes, shortly after that, we heard the same thing again. So we were thinking, "What's going on here? Are these women going to keep giving birth here?" But actually, it was them who kept coming and taking men away.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Again, when you say "them" --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Serbs soldiers. Women were screaming, children were screaming, everybody screamed. And a little later, maybe 15 minutes later, you could hear people screaming and moaning from the outside. Yes, they were moaning. Occasionally you would hear a shot, but sometimes not, and then everything would be silent for a while, and then nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did this go on much of the night?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: It lasted all night. And there were also crazy women, women who had gone round the bend there out of fear there, those whose nerves were not as strong and poor health. And I heard, I didn't see, but I heard that there were also people who hanged themselves out of fear.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, the next day, what did you do? July 13th.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: The 13th of July, when we were to go out, there were lots of people, and there was a crowd, and people were so packed that they barely made it to the barricade. And where the barricade was, they would let through perhaps 200 or 150, as many as can fit onto a truck. And there was a second barricade some 10 or 15 metres further on, which simply separated men from women and children.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Who did the separating of men from women and children?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: The Serb troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And were you trying to get you and your family onto the buses that morning?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: I tried. I followed in their steps because they were separating. I couldn't. I was carrying water to have for my children so that on the road they could have some refreshment, because there were people who were passing out. A Serb soldier grabbed me by the shoulder and said, "Here." I said, "Let me see off my children, at least, to the trucks." He says, "You can't." So I gave that canister to a grandchild. And the Serb soldier grabbed me by the shoulder, and I had to go into the house there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Why did you want to put your family and yourself on the bus that morning? Why did you want to leave?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: I wanted to go to Tuzla, to the free territory, and to go with my children and my grandchildren. My daughter-in-law couldn't manage all by herself with all of them, but she had to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Why didn't you want to leave your home that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Left because I had to. Shells were pounding for six days. On the seventh day I had to leave. The troops had left, leaving UNPROFOR withdrawing. Nobody says he's resisting, they're simply retreating inside the town. Unfortunately, and much to the disgrace of everybody, there was no support from any side. So I had to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'd like to show Witness I the Exhibit 5/17, if we could. Now, Witness I, I've showed you that photograph before. Does that building in that photograph look familiar to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: It looks -- it could have been here, this house, the house which was full. And when it filled up, the buses came, after perhaps an hour, and we sat in the bus and started for Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Before we get to the bus, I want to ask you: Could you point on this picture where you first went inside this house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: I entered here, from the road [indicates]. There's a door from the road. It could have been here [indicates], from this side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Showing that to be the right side of the picture. And when you went inside the house, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: When I entered the building, we were down on the ground floor and sitting down. The door was open. Others were driven in, and I saw them go up to the upper floor. A Serb soldier came and said, "Anybody got any marks? Give them over here." A man had them. He put his hand in his pocket and said, "Hurry up, hurry up, before somebody else comes." And he left.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were there other Serb soldiers in the house with you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Well, there were those who were escorting from the road, from the barricade into the house. So that happened to be in the house and come to the house and drive in other people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how long were you in the house, until you were taken out to the buses?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: About an hour, until enough people gathered. Half an hour, an hour, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How full was the house right before you were taken out of it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Downstairs on the ground floor, the room where I was, it was full. Well, now, how many there were on the upper floor, I couldn't say, but there were quite a lot of people there too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you see anything bad happen to anybody while you were in that house, besides what you've described?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Well, there, there -- no, not in the house. I didn't see there, but I heard. I heard that some had been driven out of the house somewhere uphill, but I didn't see.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So where were you taken when you were taken out of the house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: They took us to buses and to Bratunac, the old school, the one that had been vacated. At the time, I didn't know what its name was, but the name of the school is Vuk Karadzic, some old hero.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So did you go to Bratunac by bus or by truck?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And was your bus full of men?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And were those men that had been in the White House with you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes, from there, from the house. They were thrown out and took the buses from the house to the school Vuk Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were there any soldiers on the bus with you that took you to the school in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Well, there were two soldiers, as a rule.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were they armed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes; automatic weapons. And when we got to Bratunac and went into the school, then they forced us -- we discarded all the bags, all the food that we had. It all remained outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did they force you to discard the bags and the food that you had?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: They made us do it. And whoever had a watch, a tobacco box, or a nail, or a knife, a razor blade, they forbid us strictly to have any of those. So that I took off my coat, left it next to the bag. I just left it all and that was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You were there at that school for two nights?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes, two nights since we arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you tell us what happened to you and others at that school during those days and nights?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: It happened instantly. A Serb, sort of policeman, came and began to beat a man, and with his rifle at that, hitting him on the head from above. Blood poured down his face and his shirt. So he stayed for about an hour amongst us, with us, that bloody man. An hour later, he again came to the door, only waved at him -- only pointed at him with his finger, yelling, "Come on out here." And this one hesitated, but he had to stand up and go out. Nothing. All you could hear were cries. You could hear his cries of pain, and moans, and the voice getting weaker and weaker and weaker as the life slowly dies out. And then they did it all the time. They were taken away. It didn't matter if it was day or night. All you heard were cries of pain, moans. I dared not look out of the window to see, because if you looked, then there would be bursts of fire at you. You had to lie down not to be killed through the window.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How many people were in the room where you were kept?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Well, there could have been -- the room was largish and it was crammed. There could have been perhaps about 250, about that in that room. And in other rooms, how many there were there, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was there anything distinctive about what the soldiers or Serb personnel were wearing that were doing this to you and your fellow Muslims?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Well, only knowledge. I know that those soldiers were in multicoloured uniforms, and the one who gave the beating with the rifle on the head, he was in a sort of blue suit. He had a white military belt and his pistol with the white holster. Now, was it a military police or a civilian, I really couldn't say or no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: About how many soldiers or Serb personnel were around or inside that school during the period that you were kept there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Well, there could have been eight or ten, thereabouts. They were taking out and torturing. Sometimes a voice would die out. You couldn't hear it from the tortures. And sometimes you could even hear bursts of fire, shots, after those cries of pain.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were you allowed to go to the toilet sometimes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: We had to ask. They were in the passage, and they escorted us if we wanted to go. But as we went there and came back, they were sometimes known to hit you on the back with the rifles, so that many people suffered and tried to contain themselves because they were afraid of those blows and tried not to ask to go out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So what did they have to do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Well, had to -- because there were times when I watched a man relieve himself right there. It happened. Or perhaps takes a plastic bag or a bottle and urinates in the bottle. And the second, the third, runs, grabs the bottle. I think he wants to pee, but, no, he takes it and drinks it up, because people were so dried up. They were all black. If you didn't know a man, well, you wouldn't recognise him, so blacked they looked, our men, our prisoners who were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did they give you some water over that two-day period, the soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Soldiers, they gave water, but there wasn't enough of it. Had they not given some water, half of those people would have died there on the spot. Such a horrible thirst. I've never known that it could be so bad.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did they give you any food ever during that time in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: I was about two nights in Bratunac, and when we started, they said, "You're going to Tuzla." Then they gave us a bit of bread on the bus and some biscuits. It was so dry, so dry, as if it was just nothing but flour or sand. It just crumbled it was so dry. Our mouths' dried up. I put it in my mouth and I tried to eat. I tried to chew for about 15 minutes perhaps, so as to just moisten it a little bit and be able to swallow. And when I saw then what it looked like, I simply didn't eat it, because I couldn't really eat it, it was so dry. So that was it after two nights and a day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were there soldiers on the buses that they put you on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes, there were. At times one, at times two, because with those buses, they were getting a ride. Sometimes buses would stop and they would get off and walk. We headed through Kravica to Tuzla. They said, "We want to go." But when we got to Konjevic Polje, we started in the opposite direction, towards Zvornik. As far as I can remember, we crossed the Drina there into Serbia. We went through Serbia as far as Loznica, and there they again took us back into Bosnia, so that we travelled through Bosnia, and when we came close to Pilica, the bus stopped there. We were there for a long time. There were seven buses. I didn't count them, but another man counted them and he told me there were seven.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Excuse me one sec. Were all those buses filled with men?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Full, yes. Sitting -- we were sitting and dared not look anywhere. That is what they asked of us, to sit down and keep our heads down. When we got near Pilica, the buses stopped there, and they stayed there for quite some time, perhaps an hour, perhaps an hour and a half. Quite some time. A man was lying in the bus, in the aisle, and all they said was, "Come on. Get him up. Pull him up a little bit." Two raised him up, and they then shouted, "He's dead." So they took him off to the road, and he remained lying next to the road. One man then tried to flee from there, because he preferred a bullet to get him rather than to wait for the genocide and torture, and a burst of fire just mowed him down, and they killed him. The buses started off and arrived in Pilica. I think I know it was Pilica.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Who killed the man that tried to run away?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Serb soldiers who were guards; guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were they the ones that were on your bus or from other buses?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Well, in our bus, as they took that man out, so the soldiers came off too. They came out, this man was taken out, and this one moved here, moved there, and took to his heels. And those guards who were there with automatic armament, and so they killed him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. When you got to Pilica, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: There, as we went, we turned left. As far as I can remember, it was the school, quite large. Whether two or three-storeys high, I wouldn't know to say. We were so afraid and dared not look around or observe because our lives were at stake non-stop. And Serb troops immediately began to drive out from rooms, from my room, from other rooms, and you could only hear behind the school wails, cries for help, curses, bursts of fire. Sometimes you wouldn't even hear a shot, simply life would die out and that would be that. As we were going into the school and then up the stairs, we who were of advanced age, almost all of us had some caps on. And up the stairs they forced us and ordered, "Off with your caps," so that we all had to throw off our caps on the stairs. And I thought there, "There must be some Generals around if we have to take off our caps."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were you wearing a cap today like the one they made you take off at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes, I was. I brought it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could you just show it to us, for a second? Just raise it up for us to see it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes, I'll do that. So this is the kind of cap that we used to wear, all of us [indicates], and we had to throw them on the stairs and that's where they remained.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How crowded was the room that you were put in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't tell you exactly. There could have been around 250 people in it, but it was packed. It was overcrowded. If you stood up, after that you could no longer sit down. There was no room to sit down.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were there Muslim men in other parts of the school, could you tell?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes, there were, because I heard voices from the other door, and I heard people talking from other rooms as well. As to how many rooms there were, the crowded ones, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Roughly, how old were the people, the Muslim men, who were at this school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Let me tell you. They were from the age of 14, let's say, until 80. I am pretty sure about that. People who were much older than myself. I also noticed a man who was mute, deaf.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was there ever a time that the soldiers said anything about the younger men?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Well, yes. They said something. At one point they came in, and they asked if anybody was 15 or 16 years of age. And there were very young boys there, maybe 14. You could tell that, because they really looked young. Schoolchildren, actually. So he said, "Let me see how many you are." So they gathered at one point and lined up. I think that there were 12 of them. And the man said, "Abdic needs guys like you. They should go to him." So I don't know how many such young boys there were in other rooms, but in our room there were 12 of them. They were taken out, but what they did with them, I don't know. I don't know whether they ended up in a camp, whether they were killed later on or indeed sent to Abdic. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Who, to your understanding, was this "Abdic" that this Serb soldier mentioned?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Abdic -- I forgot his last name. He defected to Croatia. He helped both Croats and Serbs, and he hid Muslims. He worked against them. Such was the policy at that time. He was against Muslims, and he was one of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could you tell how many soldiers were around or in that school guarding you people?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me. You said Abdic was "one of them," meaning one of the Muslims or one of the Serbs? Who are "them"? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was Mr. Abdic a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Well, yes, he was a Muslim, but I'm not sure. Maybe he was from a mixed marriage, as far as I know. He was a turncoat. I don't know what actually happened between those politicians.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could you tell how many Serb soldiers there were guarding you at this school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Well, approximately there could have been between eight and ten soldiers standing at each spot. Some of them were guarding us and others were taking people out and torturing them. So this is how they would split. This is how it happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When you say "each spot," what spots do you mean?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: I mean spots around Bratunac while we were there, and also while we were in Pilica, where people were being taken out from the buses, and I'm also referring to the places where people were shot down.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I just want to concentrate right now on Pilica. Do you know how many soldiers, roughly, were guarding you at the Pilica school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: About eight or ten. I cannot tell you exactly, because they were not standing in one single group. I could not count them. Some of them were outside, some of them were in the room or in one of the corridors. There could have been approximately ten of them. If they had been in a line, I would have counted them and I would have known exactly, but I cannot give you the exact number.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were they armed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, they were. Most of them had automatic weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you describe how they were dressed, the Serb soldiers at Pilica, at the school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: As far as I know, they were dressed in some kind of multicolored clothing. That's what they wore. But, you know, I cannot really make a difference. I cannot distinguish between their clothing because I was terrified, and then, you know, it was five years ago. I just know that their clothes were multicolored.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you recall how long -- how many nights you spent at that school in Pilica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Hmm, whether it was one night or two -- I forgot. I don't know whether I stayed there one night or two nights.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were you taken someplace in the morning of the day -- sorry. Let me start over again. What happened at the school the morning before -- just before they took you out on the buses?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: What happened on that day was the following: There was one of us who asked for food, and the Serb soldier said, "We don't have anything to eat. We cannot give anything to you." So after awhile, he brought a piece of bread. He was holding it in his hand. And everyone could get just about a mouthful of bread but that was all. And he threw crumbles of that piece of bread to the people, and then he left. Whether he did the same in other rooms, I don't know. We had nothing to eat. This was just harassing us. Then after that, on that day, they asked us if we wanted to go to Sarajevo. They wanted to know if anyone had any money, and they told us that the bus to Sarajevo was 20 German marks. One of us, he said to a man who was next to him, he said, "I have 100 German marks, so I think I can pay for five of us so we can get out and reach the free territory." So whoever had any money would go out as if to go to Sarajevo, to board a bus to Sarajevo. But nobody had any money left. At one point, apparently they said that those who didn't have any money could also leave. They told us, "Well, you will go to Tuzla." Then at one point they brought two large sheets. One was white in colour and the other one was green. They gave them those two sheets to two men who were there sitting with us, and they told them to tear it into small pieces and to tie the pieces together.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Excuse me, Witness I. Could I interrupt you for a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Perhaps this would be a good time to take a break, Mr. President, and we can continue after the break.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes, we can do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. McCloskey, I agree with you. Witness I, you also need to have some rest, and after the break you will continue. You've been telling us about some terrible stories. So we will have a 20-minute break now, and after that we will continue with hearing you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We shall resume. Witness I, have you managed to have some rest?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did they offer you some coffee or something else to drink?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I had a Coke.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very good. Very good. Mr. McCloskey will continue now to ask you questions. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We had left off where someone had brought in some sheets of material and they were being torn into strips. Can you tell us who these people were that brought in these sheets of material? And then tell us about what happened.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Serb soldiers brought that and gave them to our two inmates to tear them up and then to tie people, and so they tore them and tied us. But as they were our folks, they did not tie us too tightly. But they tied our hands behind our backs. As they tied, group after group left and went outside. I offered my hands to be tied, but I was surprised, why were they tying us if we were allegedly going to freedom, to Tuzla? There was a neighbour with me and some six or seven others that I knew, and so they tied us and we started out, escorted by Serb soldiers. As we were going down the stairs and reached the ground floor, I saw a man lying on the concrete, dead, blood around him on the concrete, all spilt. We came out in a column, tied, towards the buses. We were not allowed to look anywhere. "Just keep your head down, with your hands tied, and look in front of you." When I got to the bus, I just cast a look above the bus. There were some four officers not saying a word to us, not saying anything, just talking in a quiet voice among them, casting looks at us and grinning now and then. And the Serb soldiers escorting us, pushing us, throwing foul language at us, and that's how we got onto the buses. We travelled in those buses for about two, two and a half kilometres. And on a hill, as we were moving, we heard gunfire, we heard voices. And then when we got to where this gunfire was coming from, the buses stopped, and no sooner did they stop and the doors opened. Serb troops all around the buses, "Get off now. Fuck your mothers and Alija's and everybody's. Get off. Alija doesn't want you." A group got off the bus, up to half of the bus, and then they stopped. "Enough," they said, "for the moment." And I was in that second half of the bus. I watched as the column goes down a path, and I watched to where the dead ones are. I got there and I heard Serb troops cursing, making noise. Bursts of fire simply mowed them down. They all fell to the ground. Serb soldiers came back to fetch us, that half of the bus, and drove us off the bus, as we were stepping down from the bus. So the column headed for the shooting area. As I stepped down, a Serb soldier tells me, "You, give over the marks." I said I didn't have them because I didn't, and he kicked me in the stomach. I fell to the ground, on my knees. Another Serb soldier behind my back said, "Don't commit genocide. Get your rifle and kill as the soldiers do." They forced me, and I stood up and I followed the column along. Along that path, a dead body here and there I could see. And the one who kicked me, the same one asked, "Does anyone want to say that he is a Serb so that we let him be?" and two said they would, just to stay alive, but nothing came out of it. Another one in the column, one of ours, asked, "Give us water to drink, and kill us after that," but nothing doing again. When I got to where those killed were, they were all in a row, they looked like lines which had been lodged, and there were many, many of them. And then I saw that those who had supposedly left to Sarajevo, paid for the buses, had been killed. They were giving money and then their lives. When we passed between those rows, towards the end of those rows, between them, they said, "Turn your backs and line up with them." We turned our backs and lined up. Then he orders not "Fire," he orders "Lie down," but at that moment bursts of fire cut us all down. And I fell, and they also fell, cropped down by the bursts of fire. When the gunfire stopped, then a Serb soldier asked, "Is there anyone alive?" and two made out that they were alive. One said, "I am," and another one said, "I am. Come kill me." I kept silent. If need be, I'd let them know that I'm alive later on and let them kill me then. And so column after column, they drove up there. I was lying down. They drove up some six columns more, and below me, lining them up, and bursts of fire just cropping them down. A bullet then hit me in the elbow but just grazed my skin as they were killing those others who were below me. The earth was flying about from bullets. You could hear bullets hitting bodies; and this earth flying about; stones falling around, on my back; dust all around, and I could feel it, everything, because all I had was a shirt. So when they slew them all, downed them all, they disappeared. I couldn't even hear the buses move. I couldn't hear it. They must have looked for a shade somewhere from where they drove us up there. So they must have found a shade and were having a rest. I then --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you for a moment.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes, you may.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: On the way to the killing spot, were there any Serb soldiers on your bus, from the school to the killing spot that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: At least one. I know there was one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: About how many soldiers, if you can tell us, were taking part in the executions or were at the execution fields?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: About seven, eight. Must have been about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how many --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: And they were standing up there, those who were killing, just receiving new groups and taking them away and killing them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were you able to estimate how many dead people were at that ground?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: I estimated between 1.000 and 1.500.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what happened after all the shooting finally stopped?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: When the shooting stopped, they inquired, every column, "Is there anyone alive?" Sometimes a voice is heard or two voices; sometimes nobody responds. And a soldier comes up, and just one bullet, bop, bop, and it's all over. And they go back for other columns and so on, until they killed another six columns or so. Then they went to take a rest in the shade. Then I moved my limbs to see if I was wounded, and had failed to notice that in all that fright. But, fortunately, I wasn't wounded anywhere, except that thing that grazed my arm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you hear the Serb soldiers say anything to each other?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: I didn't hear it. All I heard was shouting, using foul language, making noise, but I couldn't get what they were talking about. What with fear, you can't really follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Tell us how you were finally able to get away from this spot.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: When they went to have a rest and when I couldn't hear the buses, seeing I wasn't wounded, I tried then to get rid of those ties, and I managed to get rid of the thing that was tied around my hands. As I got rid of it, I again took it and put it back on my hands. Then I was lying on my belly and thinking so I remembered they'd be back to see, and that it would be better for me to be tied while I thought what to do. All of a sudden, a patrol came up again, and from what I could hear, there were five, judging by the voices. As soon as they arrived, one of them shouted, "There's one fleeing. There's another one. Fire." Bursts of fire, and they started up after them. One, I could hear, stayed there, walking up and down. Some time passed, and two of those came down again, came back. But the one who had stayed behind asked, "Well?" And those said, "Well, no. Those two have driven him away. He's hid somewhere. I don't know if they will find them," which man that they'd killed, the other one. And then one of them said to the other one, "We've made a genocide like it was in Jasenovac in 1941." So for a while, they walked up and down there and left again. I raised my head to see where the sun was, to see by the sun how long was it before the dark, and to see where the closest trees, woods were, to get there. But the woods was far away and the day was long. Down in the field I could see a long boundary. There was some grass. There was some bramble, some bracken, something that was overgrown, something about 100, perhaps maybe 150 square metres. So I told myself, "I'll go there." Somebody whispering not far from me. I turned my head a little, and I only said, "Well, who's alive? Get out." And I was preparing myself, because I was afraid. It was daylight still. The dredger would come or a truck to pick us up, and they'll cut me into pieces alive. So I must get out, just not to be there, because the day -- it was another two or three hours before dark. It must have been at least as much before the night. I got off those things from my hands, cast a look behind me. Two men are getting into those thorns where I wanted to get. And I can't crawl over those dead for a long time. I'm afraid a patrol will come again and see me. So I leapt to my feet. I risked, and across those dead bodies I ran, some 15 metres across the dead ones, trampling over them. Down I stumbled, was about to fall down on those bodies, and I looked at the ground and listening, all my ears open to hear somebody saying, "There's another one fleeing," because if somebody shouts that, then I'm done for. I fled to that spinney, and, fortunately, couldn't hear a voice anywhere. So I went down and into that bramble. When I looked, another two were getting into that bracken. As they got there, so they covered the entrance that we went through so that they couldn't see that. Nobody else stands up, everybody's dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So how many people were hiding in those brambles with you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Two of them that had gone there before me. Then I was the third one, then two others followed. So there were five of us. We didn't dare speak. I just asked one of them where he was from, and he said he was from the village of Jagonje, and I told him where I was from. So if we managed to cross over, if anyone survives, so that we know something about each other so that we could tell later on something about each other, but I didn't ask him his name. So a patrol appeared again and started to walk around amongst the dead and near the woods, but, fortunately, they didn't know that somebody was hiding in the brambles. So we remained there. We could hear the clicking sound of their weapons. We could hear them walk around. They also talked, but I couldn't make out what they were saying. And they stayed there until dusk, and when night fell they left. At that point, I stretched out a little bit. We found some sour berries to eat. We had not eaten for almost three days and we were half dead. We had been tied up for so long. Then after dark, when it became dark, we entered the forest on one side, and then we got out of the forest on the other side. At that point, I saw that there were dead bodies over there as well. Those people had been killed before me. Those were the ones who were supposedly going to Sarajevo, at least I believe that they were there. So we continued across the field. The area was moonlit a little bit, but I didn't know which way to go, which way we were going. We only knew where Serbia was. So we took the opposite direction, and we were trying to get deeper into Bosnia. When we reached another forest, we could no longer see anything. It was pitch dark. The others were younger than me, between 25 and 30 years of age, more or less, all four of them, and I could no longer follow them, so I stayed behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Witness I, let me ask you a few questions now, if I could.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Have you ever seen any of those four people that you became separated with that night?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: No, I didn't see. I never saw them again. I inquired about them. I asked if there had been a man from that village who had escaped the execution, the man from the village of Jagonje, the one that told me where he was from. And I was told that nobody of that description arrived, which means that the three others didn't arrive either. They must have been caught along the way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, the next morning did you find a roadway and come upon a vehicle, and can you tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes, I can tell you about that. On that evening, after they'd gone and I was left alone, I would stand up and I would only cover 50 metres, perhaps, and then I would get very tired. And I had to stop again, have a five-minute rest, and then continue. So I went on like this. I would cover only a 50-metre distance and then I would need to stop. And then I ran into some kind of ambush. As they had been executing people the night before, there was a number of patrols that were set up, and they were probably after those who were trying to flee. So I reached the road and I saw a man, some 30 metres away from me, and he asked, "Who is it?" And I started to run and I didn't say anything, I didn't respond. I couldn't go any further, but I managed to reach two houses. There was a garden, a vegetable garden, behind one of the houses, and I hid there. But the men went on shouting and yelling after me. He was sort of commanding his soldiers, "To the right," "To the left," "Close in on him," saying things like that. I followed closely, I listened carefully, and I couldn't see anyone, but I realised that I had to keep on hiding and lying down. And then he would wait for me to say something, to move. He knew that I was there but he couldn't see me because I was in the dark, in the shade. And then another man joined him and they started to whisper, to talk, and they went on talking for about five minutes. At one point one of them started to sing and simply left in the opposite direction. So I thought this was intended for me to think that they both had left, but I realised that only one had left and that the other had stayed there but was just keeping quiet. But then the other guy reappeared and I could see him above me, and he started yelling again and he fired his rifle two times, I don't know in which direction, and then he disappeared again. I could tell what he was trying to do. He was trying to trick me, but he didn't manage so he left the area. So I went back to my hiding place and I managed to reach the area above the road, and this is how I spent that night. It was very difficult. I was alone. I couldn't see anything; I couldn't see which way I was going. I would fall down, and then it would be difficult for me to get out of the bushes. When the day broke, I reached one area of the forest, near the field, and I stayed there for a while, to have some rest. Again I was trying to find some food --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If I can just interrupt you. Could you tell us now, this next day, about the vehicle you saw, and try to tell us as you feel the important parts are, but remember, we don't want you to testify -- we want you to be able to finish your testimony today. So if you could tell us the most important parts of that story, when you see the vehicle, and then we'll go on from there.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes, I can do that. So I spent the night there and the following day, I stayed there, and after that I wanted to move, to leave the area. And at one point I heard a vehicle engine and I realised that the vehicle was not moving. And I couldn't go on, I couldn't go any further. I also heard some noise, people talking, and I then set out in the opposite direction. But I knew I had to reach the road, because after about 20 metres there again would be a forest which I could use. I came to the road and I looked down the road, and I realised that there was blood on the road. There was a bloodstain which was about half a metre wide and a few other smaller stains of blood on the road, and I thought that they were probably driving away the dead that had been killed on the previous day. So I managed to reach the wood, and I was about to turn and then all of a sudden a truck appeared from down below. And when it came close, I looked at it and I realised that it was filled up with bodies, dead bodies. When this truck was close to me, when it came next to me, when I was about to turn into the forest, then I heard a voice say, "This is the one that escaped yesterday." As soon as I heard that, I was confused but I realised that I shouldn't go, shouldn't turn into the forest at that point, because they would catch me. There was no way for me to escape, so I decided to continue along the road, and that was a tricky part because I didn't know what would happen on the road. So I continued along the road, pretending I was crazy, drunk, tired. I hurried up a little bit but I wasn't fleeing. I didn't turn back towards the truck, but I could tell that the truck had stopped, and it stopped maybe 30, 40 metres away from me. And then one man came out of the truck, and at that moment I was already a bit further. I had already reached a bridge and I crossed that bridge, and I still wasn't turning around. I didn't want to let him know that I was fleeing. I pretended I was a free citizen walking around. So after a while I did turn just a little to see what was going on, and it was at that moment that the man turned away from me, because he was following me, he was watching me, trying to see whether I would flee. But then apparently he thought that I was just a free man walking around and he apparently no longer had any doubts. And then he turned towards the truck and started actually to run after the truck, and then the engine was started and they left. And at that moment I ran towards a brook, and this is where I stood, this is where I remained, and I waited for the dusk. After the night fell I went back to the point where I wanted to reach the forest, where I wanted to turn into the forest. And this is what I did. So I walked through the woods for a while, not far from a field. It was already night; it was completely dark. I was trying to get some rest, trying to figure out what to do. I was in an unknown land. I was alone. I just didn't know what to do. But then all of a sudden a figure appeared, a man came to me, and I was terribly frightened because I didn't know who it was. He had his hands in his pockets, and he gave me some water. He told me, "Have some water," and I realised that he had also fled like myself --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Excuse me, Witness I. Can you tell me only the first name of that man?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Becir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You were finally able to, with Becir, escape. Can you tell us about the day that you and Becir decided to turn yourselves in, and tell us how that happened.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: We wanted to surrender. At that time there was one other man who was with us, we ran into him in the woods, so there were three of us. So we continued on foot for a while. While we were still in the woods, this other guy, the third man, went to fetch some food, but apparently he got lost. And then we heard some shots, so we thought that he was dead. We started travelling again on the following night, and having covered quite a distance from the spot where the execution had taken place, we realised that we were very tired, that we were about to faint. We were very weak. We had nothing to eat, only some sour berries and unripe apples. Our mouths were aching, and the berries were so sour that our mouths were like wounds. So we were in a lot of pain. So this is how we decided to surrender ourselves. Otherwise, we would die. There was no other option, no way out. So we came up to the road again and we saw a man passing by in civilian clothes. He saw us and he got frightened immediately because he realised that we were not one of theirs, because we looked completely dishevelled. We were in a terrible state. So he started asking questions and he wanted to know where we were from, and we told him that we were from Srebrenica and we told him, "You know what's happened in Srebrenica. Now we just want to surrender to your authorities, the Serb authorities." He wanted to know whether we had any weapons, rifles, hand grenades. He inquired whether there were many more of us in the woods. And we wanted to ask him to give us a lift, but he said he couldn't. He had no time, he had some other business to do, and he told us to go down there and that we would find someone there. So we went down the road and reached the spot where some people were standing. They told us that a bus would be coming, and after a few minutes a bus, indeed, came. So we boarded the bus and we saw two policemen and a driver on the bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were these civilian policemen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes, civilian policemen. At least that's what I think. They were wearing blue uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were you taken to a little cafe where a Serb person helped you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes. They were walking around, and at one point they went to a cafe, the two policemen. They got into the cafe. I saw some people sitting outside the cafe, drinking, smoking, and when they learned about us -- meanwhile, we were still on the bus, which was parked some 20 metres from the cafe. So when they learned about us, when they realised who was on the bus, the guy went back into the cafe and then he came back with two packs of cigarettes and one litre of juice, and he came with these two policemen to give us some cigarettes. And said, "Have a cigarette. Have some juice." This was so good for us. This saved us. I will never forget what this man did to us. He said, "I treat everybody the in same way. I used to work in Germany. I like everyone. I respect everyone." And he said, "Are you hungry?" I said, "Yes, we are. We haven't seen a piece of bread in 15 days." Then this waiter said, "Well, come to the cafe." So we went to the cafe. We sat outside the cafe, and he gave us a very good lunch, which consisted of a piece of meat, some bread, some stock, and we ate that. It was only lukewarm, but my mouth was burning as if it had been cut. I managed to eat something, but the guy who was with me took only two mouthfuls because he couldn't eat any more. His stomach was aching. So after we had lunch, the man offered us some coffee. While we were drinking coffee, the policeman told us to hurry up, that we had to go. So after we had coffee, we left. This man, this waiter, was so precious for us, and I will never forget him. I didn't dare ask him about his name, his last name, but today I would really like to know his name. He was like a good friend of mine. He behaved like a man. So we went on. We went back to the buses and left. At one point, I heard someone said that -- we were sitting in the back of the bus, and then another voice telling him, "Well, we should take them off the bus and finish them off." I don't know who said that. I don't know if it was the driver or one of the policemen, but this is what I heard at that moment. Then at that point the policemen stood up and came to us. Then one of them brandished a knife and threatened my colleague. He wanted to cut off his ear. He put a gun barrel against my forehead and he wanted me to give him German marks, but I didn't have any. I just had to keep silent. But he shouted again, "Give me your marks." And I said, "I don't have any." Then they looked at each other, smiled a little, and then went back to their places at the front. This is now we reached Karakaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Shortly after that, were you put on a truck with some other Muslim prisoners and taken to Batkovic prison in Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Well, I arrived there to Karakaj, and they said, "Come, report to the command, police," or what do I know. And we got off, but before I made three or four steps, he shouted, "Come. Come back. Come back. Come back to the truck. You'll go with this one." So I did come back onto that truck, and there was the canvas all around. The only part where you got onto it was open and there were another 20 or so, those who had come from Srebrenica to Zvornik and had been caught somewhere there, and the two of us -- 29 altogether. One said -- "It's all right," he said. "There's Red Cross escorting us." So we set off towards Batkovici, and the Red Cross was also coming with us, escorting us. When we reached Batkovici, we entered there and there were many other people who had been caught.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you know about what day this was that you came to Batkovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: I think it was the 26th. 26th. No, I don't think it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When were you finally released from that prison?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: We were then registered and spent five months there, and when the sixth month came, it was the exchange, on the 24th of November, right before the New Year. That was when I was exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I want to take you back, briefly, to the execution site. Were there any particular buildings or other prominent objects there that you recall? I know you weren't able to see much because of the situation, but you've always recalled that -- something prominent that you recall. What was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: I remember well where we got off. Where we got off was something like an apple tree. Further on one could see a garden or a vegetable garden. Whether there was a house there or not, I don't know, because we were not allowed to look much around. We had to look in front and keep our heads down. So what else was there, I don't know. Where I was at the execution site, I saw the spinney in that direction. I could see two buildings, and I could see men making noise near those buildings, shouting, yelling, perhaps at some cattle, at some livestock. Was he feeding them, giving them to drink, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much, Witness I.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Visnjic, how long do you think you will need, more or less, for the cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I don't think I will need more than half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right. So it would be better if we made a break now and then we shall come back to it. Therefore, we shall make a 20-minute break, and we will resume with the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness I, I should like to remind you, when you finish your testimony, don't leave immediately because our protective measures need to be put in order then. So now you will answer questions which Mr. Visnjic will ask. Mr. Visnjic is a sensitive person and he'll treat you well. Now you will answer his questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness I.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Before I begin, with my questions, I should like to ask you, since the two of us speak the same language, to just wait a little before you give your answer after you've heard the question, so that the interpreters, who are interpreting into English and French, will have time to cover both my question and your answer. A purely technical matter.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Witness I, I know it is very hard for you to go back and relive those events, and I shall try to be as precise as I can, and I will ask you now the following: In your testimony today, you described your stay in Potocari in the night between the 12th and the 13th of July. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: No, no. I will ask you. That was the second night?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes, the second night.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: You said that Serb soldiers were taking away Muslim men during the night.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: My question is very short. Did you see with your own eyes the Serb soldiers take away people or did you hear it from other people who were with you in the area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: I heard that from other people. And that night I personally heard screams, wailing, people screaming, crying for help, and that sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes. My second question: When you were in that house that you recognised on the photograph that the Prosecutor showed you, in Potocari too, you were guarded there by Serb soldiers; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes. In that house, they were separating, bringing people in, and, yes, walking up and down and guarding.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Could you describe their uniform?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: All I can describe is many coloured clothes. Other things, I know nothing about that. But there were all sorts of those clothes and they were all of many colours.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: When you say "many colours," you mean camouflage, olive-green/grey?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Well, yes, something like green and blue, those colours, many of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And from that house, when you headed for Bratunac by bus, by bus to Bratunac --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: -- were those the same soldiers who escorted you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Why, I don't know. I didn't know those soldiers, can't give you their names and say "so and so" and "so and so" and "so and so" were there. I don't know. They didn't allow us to look at them, so a man can't recognise them. That must have been why they wouldn't allow us to look at them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: The soldiers who were on the buses and arrived in Bratunac with you, and those who put you in that school, Vuk Karadzic, did they also guard you during those two days that you spent there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Well, yes, they guarded us throughout. And not only that, but they also took us out and killed us, and there were screams in that school. But it was not the same soldiers all the time. One day, two nights, nobody could manage that. They must have had two shifts, 100 per cent. But shifts, as they came -- when they came, every shift did the same thing. They didn't do as the army should do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you a question, my next question: From the school in Bratunac, you were taken to Pilica. Could you tell us, do you think it was those same soldiers who were in Bratunac with you? You can answer it only with yes or no. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: I can't answer because they had shifts, that's why I'm saying that. They brought us to Bratunac. Perhaps one shift went to have a break and another shift came, "You're all right. You'll move on to Tuzla." But it all happened the other way around; they said one thing and did a different thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Witness I, did you notice, while you were in Pilica, did you notice a soldier -- let me try it this way: Did you notice in Pilica any of the soldiers that you saw in Bratunac or in Potocari, or any of the soldiers that you saw in the buses either between Bratunac and Pilica or between Potocari and Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: I only know those who came from Bratunac to Pilica on the buses with us, who escorted us there, and there were other troops there who took us over. And with those who escorted us on that road, I don't know what happened to them. Whether they stayed there or went back or went on, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: So in Pilica you were met by some new soldiers that you had not seen before.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Well, as soon as we got off, there were many troops there, I could see there were many troops there, and they took us to the school right away.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My next question is: Did the soldiers who met you at Pilica wear different uniforms from the soldiers that you saw in Bratunac and Potocari?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Well, it was similar -- same uniform, I mean clothes. And weapons too, mostly automatic weapons, a carbine here and there or a PAP, the automatic one.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Witness I, my next question is: You told us that between Pilica and the place of the execution, in every bus there was at least one soldier.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes, escorting, in the bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Those soldiers, would they get off together with the group and stay at the site of execution, or did they go back with the buses? Could you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: They were down at the school, those who saw us to the buses, and they would go back to the school and take another group. And a soldier, say, who would escort us in the bus, he would come out up there for the execution, and they only stood there. They were there and they were executing there. They were executing there. They were meeting every bus as it would come, and execute everybody, shoot everybody, and they were always there, that group. That group did not go --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes. That group of soldiers which performed the executions, did they perhaps wear uniforms different from the ones that you saw on other people, or did they have, perhaps, any special patches?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: I could not see any other patch. But it was also, you know, great fear. Lives are disappearing. You don't think about anything else. You're counting your life by minutes and by seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My next question: You said that when you surrendered you were escorted by the civilian police. What uniforms did they have?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: I think they were civilian because the clothes were blue, that's why I think so, not many colours like the troops, like the military had, but blue. They were quite young men, and I can be quite satisfied with that police. Yes, they did harass us a little bit, pistol to the forehead. But all right, I mean, people want marks, and others want marks and take both your marks and your life. So that's that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Just one more question, and that is my final one, Mr. President. In your testimony you said that at the place of execution one of the soldiers mentioned Jasenovac in 1941.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes, a Serb soldier mentioned that, a Serb soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Could you explain to the Chamber, what was Jasenovac? Jasenovac was a concentration camp, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: I don't have enough school to know about that, but from what I've heard, a major massacre happened there once in 1941. But who died there and how he died there, I don't know because I don't have much school.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the victims of that massacre were Serbs, Jews, and Romanies or Gypsies?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: I wouldn't know that, but from what I think, I suppose, yes, Jews, and perhaps Serbs too. But I wouldn't really know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Visnjic. Mr. McCloskey, do you have any additional questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Riad, do you have any questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Witness I -- I have to call you "Witness I"; I shall not say your name -- good morning. Can you see me? Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Now I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You can hear me now. Good morning.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes, I can hear you now. Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Witness I, we fully realise how painful it must be for you to recount all these tragic events and to relive it again. You're a man of great courage, and we are highly grateful to know that you got out alive from these horrors. But we also deplore very much the disappearance of the others.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So accept that I will just continue these questions for a few minutes, if you can take it. Some you might need to answer and some you don't need to answer. In general, you mentioned twice that the soldiers around you were speaking of something of genocide. Did they use the word "genocide"? Is there a word in Serbo-Croat for genocide which has that meaning, or was it just killing? You said twice that they spoke of genocide; first, when you fell on the ground and one wanted to kill you, the other told him, "Wait. You should do genocide properly." And another time they spoke of something strange, a soldier told another, "Now w have done the same genocide as in Jasenovac in 1941." What was the genocide in Jasenovac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I understand. The genocide, meaning very many people were killed, perhaps even women, children. Just too many people killed. What should not have been and what should not have happened, that was done. That is the genocide. And you understand it better than I do. But I also know what it means when you butcher or torture. Because they had my son there, and if there was a choice, I would have said, "Kill me and leave my son." I would have given my life for my son.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Just tell us about this genocide of Jasenovac. Do you know something about it, in 1941, which you heard the soldiers saying?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Well, I do, but all I know is that there was a genocide in 1941 and that they were executed like in Srebrenica this time, that very many people were killed and slain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Many people? Who were they? Who did it? Was it the Serbs? Was it the Croats? Was it the Muslims? Who was killed and who was killing, if you know about it? And why were they mentioning it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: I know they knew about that genocide, seeing that they talked like that, and I was lying down then. And it was then that I heard it with my own ears, and I heard it well. Not that I noticed; I heard it with my own ears. And later on they said that Serbs, Jews had been killed there, something like that, but I don't know exactly. But, yes, it did happen. Yes, it did happen, and I know that that is so in history.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Good.
