Now, if you look at all the series of transportation from one place to another, and the killings in several places, did you feel that there was some kind of systematic organisation and, more or less, harmony in the execution, and not just something happening in a completely, let us say, wild way by criminals, by bands of criminals? Did you feel an organisation, a systematic military organisation, or criminals catching you here and there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: It surely was the order from the top, from the chiefs who ordered that, because that could not be done without their order. It was not a small genocide, it was a big genocide. All those men, 8.000. There were 8.000 Srebrenica people, and they are all gone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Speaking of numbers, you mentioned something like between 1.000 and 1.500 killed when the soldiers were executing. How do you know this number?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: I don't know the exact number. That is why I tell you between 1.000 and 1.500. There must have been, judging by this area, this surface that was covered by bodies. And 8.000 Srebrenica inhabitants are missing, and we must all know that. We must all know that there must have been children, poor people, between 16.000 and 20.000. And one needs to feed them all, to bring them up. There are so many fathers without sons, and sons without fathers. I had two sons, and I don't have them any more. Why is that? And I lived and worked in my own home, not in anybody else's, and that was -- the same held true of my father and my grandfather. But what they seized, what they took away, what they grabbed. I had two houses. One they burnt down. It could burn. They burnt it down. But the other one they couldn't burn, so they came and put a mine to it, because the house was new and I hadn't finished it yet. The roof was still missing, but it was all made of concrete and bricks, so it wouldn't burn. And I thought, "Well, it will survive at least." But, no, they came and planted mines, and it just went down. Nothing but dust. But, right, never mind that. I had it, so it's gone. They took it. They seized it. But why did they have to kill my sons? And I stand today as dried as that tree in the forest. I could have lived with my sons and with my own land, and now I don't have either. And how am I supposed to live today? I don't have a pension or anything. Before that, I relied on my sons. They wouldn't have left me. They wouldn't have left me to go hungry. And today, without my sons, without land, I'm slowly starving. Isn't that sad?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You are a man of great courage, and you survived by miracle, and this miracle will help you live.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: No. I don't understand one thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: I don't understand one thing. I simply can't understand how is it that I've kept my sanity, that I have not really gone mad. I don't understand how I got away. I really wonder to this day. I wonder to myself, "How was it possible that I got away?" I can't believe myself that I could have gone through all this, but I did go through all that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Well, if you want to have some rest, you will, but there must be a purpose for your survival; to tell the world your story. The world was waiting to hear your story.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Well, yes, it could be that. Yes. Something looked after me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So continue telling your story, which is of great value.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: I'm terribly sorry. I know you have it very hard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Rest as much as you can. But you are here to tell us something important, and we thank you for it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Serbs were my neighbours. We were all mixed altogether, all equal, and we all lived properly like neighbours should. When the politics started, what happened? I simply -- it's completely beyond me. We never quarrelled. It was easy to live while Tito ruled. We can say that then we lived well, and at that time I know that I lived a life. Today, I don't live. I live like a beast today, like a wild beast. Today, I'm not happy that I'm alive. All I'm saying, "But help me, Lord, not to suffer any more as long as I live." And I won't be sorry to die, because I see that all the good life is already behind me. All those people that I cared about are gone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I'm sorry we provoked all these memories, but we are happy that you are alive and that you are here. Now, just for a few more minutes, try to continue remembering some of your sad, tragic events. You mentioned something about -- of course, sometimes there are real kind human beings, like the man who received you in the cafe. Then you said after that you took the bus, and the people in the bus said, "We must finish them off," and the man put the gun in your forehead and the other wanted to cut the ear off your friend. Who were these people? Were they policemen or were they normal Serb citizens or soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Those were soldiers -- no, not soldiers, police. I mean, civilian police. Blue clothes is what they wore. Now, whether they were military police or civilian police, I don't know, but they looked like civilian police, blue clothes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And they wanted to finish you up. They wanted to kill you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Well, that's what one said. And the other one, what he said -- no, they did not take us anywhere. It means the other one wouldn't let him, so that we stayed there and reached Karakaj. And the Red Cross was there, and then we were taken further on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now, when you fell down after the execution, there were -- they passed to shoot everybody who was moving, and you were able not to move at all, or were you hidden under other people? If you remember. How did they not notice you, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: They did not notice because I was lying on my stomach, and I just stayed -- I raised a little bit and I just stayed like that. I did not move at all. So I was lying with my stomach down to the ground to breathe, so that one couldn't notice from my back that I was still breathing. They walked around and finished off a couple of those who were still alive, but they didn't stay long there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: But the others shouted and said they were alive, to be killed. They wanted to be killed and to finish up.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: They wanted, yes, to have it done and over with. Why? I don't know, but I suppose they must have been severely wounded. They must have had grave wounds, and that was why they called out. But I wasn't hurt. I didn't feel hurt, so I just kept silent. I thought, well, perhaps if I can't untie my hands, perhaps I will let them know that I was alive and let them kill, but I did manage to get my hands free, so that I just kept silent and stayed there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Very good. No, when you fell, did you fall because you received a bullet, or you managed to fall so that you pretended? Did the bullet reach you when they were shooting or you were hurt afterwards?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: There was not an explicit command like "Shoot." What they said was "Lie down." But it all happened at the same time. The gun burst and the command. So I fell down right after that, and I heard a burst of gunfire. At the moment I fell down, others fell down as well. But this is what they said before they opened fire, "Lie down." And I managed to fall down, and I managed to remain lying like that. After that, they kept bringing in other people, columns of other people. It was later on that I was grazed by a bullet, but only grazed. It just scratched my skin a little bit, that's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Just a last question. You mentioned that they brought children of the age of 14, they called boys of 14 and 15 years old and told them that Abdic needs them, and you said that Abdic was a man who was apparently -- we didn't know what he is, but he was fighting against the Bosnians. Do you know what happened to these children? Were they killed? Were they sent to Abdic? Did people find out after that? What were they doing to these children?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: They took 12 of them from the room. I don't know how many of them there were in other rooms, but they must have gathered them together. I don't know how many in total they were, but there were 12 of them that were taken out from our room. They said that Abdic needed them. After that, they took them out. I don't know what they did with them, whether they ended up in a camp or whether they were eventually sent to Abdic or killed, I don't know, but they haven't been heard of to this date. We don't know what's happened with them, with those children, whether they're in a camp somewhere. We know nothing about their fate. On top of that, if you think of those 8.000 men from Srebrenica, nobody can prove anything. We don't know what's happened to them. But today, all we can see is just graves everywhere, and I don't know how many more graves there are still that haven't been opened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now, when you were put on buses, if you remember, you mentioned that you crossed the Drina River into Serbia. So the bus went into Serbia --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: -- with you as prisoners in it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Not in Bosnia, in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: We went to Zvornik, and this is where we crossed into Serbia. And we travelled in Serbia for a while, up to Loznica, more or less. At that point there is a bridge over the Drina, and this is where we were -- this is where we crossed into Bosnia. We spent some time travelling through Bosnia and towards Pilica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Did anyone stop you in Serbia, in the Serbian state? Did anybody stop you, policemen or anything? Because this --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: I don't remember that. I don't remember anyone stopping us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: But it was obvious that these were buses of prisoners. And nobody stopped you there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Nobody --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: There was seven buses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Packed with you prisoners in it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes. Seven buses plus probably later on more buses came. Maybe even more buses had come before us, because I had seen a number of dead bodies before. So this may have happened before and after. Between 1.000 and 1.500. I'm sure about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And you don't remember how much time this took, the time you spent in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: We didn't spend any time there, we just travelled through Serbia for a while. We didn't stop. Maybe the asphalt road through Serbia was better, I don't know. I don't know why we went there, but we just passed through Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Witness I, thank you, and I apologise, I have added a bit to your ordeal here, but you have done a great job. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Thank you too. I really appreciate that such a Tribunal has been created. I'm very happy that we have it. I think each individual should be held responsible for what he has done, because if we let this go, then lots of other things might happen again. But if we have a Tribunal like this, I think it will be better. We still cannot go back to Srebrenica. They've killed so many people and still they wouldn't let us go back to Srebrenica. We live in other people's houses. There's nothing we can call our own, and my own land is still there. They have to be captured, all of them. Then, maybe, we could go back to Srebrenica. Until that time, there will be no security. The soldiers, the police, this is all to no avail. They're unable to protect every single civilian who would like to go back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness I, we haven't finished yet. I think that Judge Wald would also like to ask a few questions of you. Judge Riad, thank you very much for your questions. Judge Wald, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Witness I, I don't have but four short questions for you. I too much appreciate your coming here. During the time that you were in Potocari, in the house with the other men, and later on in the Bratunac school and later still in the Pilica school --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: -- did anybody ever interrogate you? Did any of the Serb soldiers ever take you out and ask you questions about anything or did you just stay with the other men?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: We just stayed there inside with the other men. As for those other people who were taken out and killed, I don't know. I don't know how they were killed, whether they were killed with clubs or something else. They must have been asked something. They must have been interrogated, but they didn't want to interrogate them only, they wanted to beat them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: As for us who were inside, they didn't ask us anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: They knew all they wanted to know, that we were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Right. Could you tell, as to the men that were taken out in the Bratunac school or the Pilica school that were singled out and taken out and back and either beaten or subsequently killed, could you tell when they were called out, were they called out by name? Did somebody have a list that singled them out or did the soldiers just appear and say, "You and you and you"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Well, something like that. They would simply say, "You, get out." I didn't see any list. I didn't see them look up a list or anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: So it looked as though they were just picking them out at random? Okay.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes, I think. I think they picked up younger men and more prominent ones, and they tortured them. Those who remained were taken out, put onto buses, and executed. They didn't ask anyone anything, if they were guilty of something or not. They had camps. They could have taken people to their camps and spared their lives, but they didn't want to know anything. They just killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: When you were in the Pilica school, you said that there were people packed in the rooms. In the room you were in, you said maybe 250 men were there and that they were guarded by all around eight to ten soldiers. Was there some reason, before you were tied up, before they brought in the sheets for tying your hands, was there some reason why, with so many men, 250 in a room, they didn't feel they could overcome the seven or eight soldiers that were there and escape as a whole group, since they were so many more of them than the soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Let me tell you, that's why they had been keeping us hungry for about three or four days. They just gave us, at one point, some dry biscuits to eat. But they wanted to exhaust us as much as possible so that people would die before they had to kill them. Then on the other hand, we kept hoping that things would turn out right for us. There were just too many of us. We simply couldn't believe that people would be held accountable for something, but obviously they had a different idea in mind. All we knew was what they actually told us. They told us that we would be going to Tuzla, but they acted differently. And it was only when they started cursing us, cursing our balija mothers, it was only then that we realised that we would be killed. Until that time we were trying to behave, we would try to act normally, but then we realised that we would be killed at one point, when our hands were tied up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: My last question to you is: After the terrible ordeal that you had, both on the killing fields and later on trying to escape, what was it that made you decide in the end you would surrender? Did you think you would have a better chance of not coming back in the hands of the same soldiers, or you were just totally exhausted? What made you decide, after you'd gotten that far, that you'd give yourself up to the authorities?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Well, I was thinking, I knew I had a long way to travel, I knew that there were minefields. And we had moved away from the execution site and we thought, "Well, they cannot go on killing forever." And we were so exhausted, we could no longer walk. We were losing consciousness. We had nothing to eat, no bread, nothing, just sour berries from the forest. So it was either to die in the woods or to surrender. We didn't know the road; we didn't know the way. We couldn't orient ourselves, and we had nothing to eat. So to surrender was the only option, it meant life, and the other option was death. And this is how we surrendered. And when I came to Batkovic, for a while I didn't say anything, I didn't tell them where I was from and what I had been through, because even though the Red Cross was there, even though I had been registered, I think they would have taken me away and killed me. They didn't know about that. They didn't have this information about me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Why did they think you had -- so what did you tell them that you were surrendering for? Why did they put you in prison if they didn't know this information?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Well, they put me in prison together with other people who had come from Srebrenica and who had been captured, and this is what I told them. I told them that that was my case as well, because I didn't dare tell them anything else. And this is how I was registered and how I remained there. Because, yes, the Red Cross is a useful thing, no doubt about that, but many people had an opportunity to see how things work because they had to go out to dig trenches, people who were with us in the camp, and their identity cards, Red Cross identity cards, were taken away from them and torn apart. And after they had come back to Batkovic, the Red Cross wanted to see their cards, and there was a corporal there who said, "Don't show them, don't tell them. Just tell them you've lost them," so that they wouldn't know that the soldiers had actually torn them apart and thrown them away. And this is how they were actually forced to tell them that they had lost their identity cards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness I. We're glad you chose the option of life. We think you've done a great service. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness I, my questions for you will be very short. At the beginning you mentioned a kind of trumpet that you heard in Potocari on the 12th of July. Do you remember who it was that used that trumpet?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: I wouldn't know whether it was a Muslim, a Serb. I don't know who it had been given to. I don't know. I don't remember the clothes the man wore. It could have been a civilian suit. But it was so long ago that I have forgotten it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness I, you spoke about an execution site and you mentioned six columns of people at that execution site. Do you know, by any chance, how many people there were in each column?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: I think that approximately one bus full of people, that is, 45 seats, there were probably lots of people standing, two columns would be formed out of one bus. So there must have been 50 people on each bus, that is, between 23 and 27 people per column. It must have been like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you remember the time of the day when the executions started?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you exactly when it was, but it was in the morning hours, perhaps around 9.00 or 10.00, after they had asked people if they wanted to go to Sarajevo. At that moment, they left and then buses started coming. They kept coming and going relatively quickly, so that was kind of interesting because it was a long way to Sarajevo, and this surprised us. We had no idea how long we would live, but we kept hoping. And when they told us to get out, when they started cursing us, then we realised that there would be no life for us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My last question for you, Witness I, concerns Bratunac and Pilica, that is, the soldiers who were there. Mr. Visnjic wanted to know whether those were the same soldiers. I should like to know whether they had the same uniforms. You said that at Potocari they had had multicoloured uniforms. Did all of them have the same kind of uniform, or is it your recollection that they had changed uniforms in the meantime?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Well, all I remember was that there were soldiers wearing multicoloured suits, and then on the other hand the police who were wearing blue uniforms. These are the two kinds of clothing that I remember. I don't remember anything else. I was so afraid, so terrified, I just couldn't observe all that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, Witness I, I fully understand that. What you have told us here, Witness I, is indeed an extreme type of human conduct. It goes beyond all horror films that have been made so far. But on the other hand, there is a humane story that you have told us here too. Remember the waiter that you mentioned, you said that he had told you that he liked everyone, that he liked all people. You're a wise man, Witness I, you have experienced a lot in life, and all I can tell you at the end of your testimony is that I hope that once you go back to your country, you will no longer feel as a dry tree standing alone in the forest and that you will manage to find new hope and that this tree will live again. Witness I, this is the end of your testimony. Thank you very much for coming here to testify before the Tribunal. Let me tell you once again that we greatly admire your courage. Please do not move for the moment because we have to respect the protective measures that have been approved. Please wait for the usher to lower down the blinds so that you can leave the courtroom as a protected witness. Thank you very much, Witness I.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Harmon, or somebody else, we are ready for a new witness. Do you think it is worthwhile beginning his testimony? We have 40 minutes left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, we do have another witness, and it is another victim with evidence in the same fashion that you've heard for the last few hours. Last night when I spoke with him, he was very fragile. He has a great deal of courage but he was very fragile. He has been waiting this morning for several hours to come. In a sense, I think it may actually be worthwhile commencing testimony, because then he will at least become accustomed to the courtroom and he's not going to worry all weekend long about coming back, because he's been waiting now in a room. I think that's probably the best way to proceed, but I will leave it to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The thing is my colleagues have asked for a short break, a ten-minute break, before we start again. Can we start again at 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you hear me, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You will now read the solemn translation that the usher will show you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can take your seat now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The representative of the Registry will now show you a piece of paper with your name on it. You will look at it to see whether this is, indeed, your name, but you will only say yes or no. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do. I do. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So it is your name on that piece of paper.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Witness. Thank you very much for coming here. We know that you had a very long wait, and now you will begin your testimony. You will first answer questions that Mr. Cayley, who is to the right of you, will ask. Mr. Cayley, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours, learned counsel. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, Witness, first of all, you are perfectly safe. You are under the protection of the Judges and the court. Your image cannot be seen by anybody except the people who are in the courtroom. I'm going to ask you a few preliminary questions, and then once I've asked those, I will place you at a certain location in time and in space and then I'll ask you to tell the account of events that you told me to the Judges. Now, Witness, I think you were born in 1944; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And you are a Muslim by faith.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And I think in 1995 you were a member of the Bosnian army.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I want you to think back to the 11th of July, in 1995, and I think you were working as a farmer in your field.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And the fields on which you were working were in your local commune, which was a village that was located within the Srebrenica enclave; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And I think while you were working in the field, on the 11th of July, your daughter came to see you and she told you that the enclave had fallen. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think that you then returned home and you packed some food and you left.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges, slowly, in your own time, everything that happened to you after you left your home and your village, in the municipality of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Please go head, Witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Before we begin, I should like to thank the Hague Tribunal and the Court which enabled the truth to be told about the genocide of the Bosniaks in the protected enclave of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Witness, you can now begin with your account of events after you left your village in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: I started on the 11th of July, 1995, I left my home, between 7.00 and 8.00 in the afternoon [sic]. I put my belongings in a backpack and headed for Tuzla. When we reached Spasonjin Do, we were told that there would be a rally at Jaglici. We arrived at Jaglici at night and spent the night at Jaglici. In the morning, on the 12th of July, at twenty minutes to one was when I left Jaglici, towards Buljim. Below Buljim we came across a macadam road, and that was the first ambush. So people scattered there, nobody looked where somebody else was going, and with a few of my neighbours, I started down a stream. I didn't know the ground there; I was not familiar with it. We were walking downstream, far away, and I asked, "Where should we go?" I asked my neighbour, "Do you know where we are?" and he said, "Kamenica is to our left." So we set off to the left, through a forest, and we sat down there. About seven, eight, maybe ten men gathered there, and we were sitting down, and we heard voices from us further in the forest. It was at nightfall, so we headed towards those voices in the forest. Some 500 or 600 metres later, gunfire started, and that is where the second ambush was. You don't know what is firing or where it is firing from. So we went back. They were all younger than I. I went down behind a fallen tree trunk to protect myself, and the gunfire went on. I thought they were also lying down near me. So then I stood up and tried to call to them softly, but none of them responded. Then I heard a voice to carry the wounded away, and I thought they were ours. I headed towards them. The gunfire was going on, but it was less intensive. It would be a burst here and there. And I shouted, "Don't fire. They are ours." "Who are you?" I said -- I went up, and I found a guy. He asked me if I had any food to give him. I gave it to him. He ate. We stood up. There were so many dead bodies around, you could put -- as you walked, could you move over the dead bodies. I spent the night at a neighbour's, and I lost my way -- I lost that guy to whom I had given food. So we took the wounded up on a hill. I don't know which hill. In the morning, when the day broke, there were a number of people I knew from my neighbourhood community, from my neighbourhood, and I asked there, "Are there any more of ours?" So we started downhill, and he told me that yes, there were quite a number of ours down there. So we climbed down, and I found there quite a number of our men, so that a large group met. There was quite a number of people I knew. They were bringing wounded there. I knew a male nurse. They used to work in the hospital in Srebrenica. So they dressed the wounds there, and we were sitting there, and then the fire was opened from behind our backs. It was somewhere up from above Kamenica. We went downhill. They were falling all around us, but the grass was very tall around. Whether it was hitting them or whether they were falling down so as to avoid those, to dodge the bullets. The bullets were whizzing past my head, so I also started to roll down. I rolled down to a boundary. Then crossfire started from the other side, from the asphalt road. And they began putting their T-shirts and their towels on sticks, whatever, "Don't shoot. Don't shoot. We're surrendering. We're surrendering." but they kept on firing. The fire was coming. They were closer to us, and there they surrounded us and pushed us towards the asphalt. I don't know what the name of that place was where they drove us to, because I didn't know that place, but there was a meadow, and in the meadow there were a lot of people there, but they were driving in more of them. There were two soldiers of theirs when we crossed the river, and they said, "If you have a backpack, a bag, a plastic bag, anything," they would take it, search your pockets, the belt, naturally, to see if you had a knife or a pistol or something, some money. I had a hundred marks in my pocket here, and I took it out. I said, "That's all I have." We crossed the asphalt road and sat on the right-hand side of the asphalt, in a meadow, and they were still driving people into that meadow. There were troops, their troops around us. They did not beat us. We were sitting --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Witness, if you could pause there for a moment, and I want to ask you some questions about the evidence that you've given to the Judges, just to clarify it in my mind. Now, you've said earlier on that on the 1th of July, 1995, you went to a place called Jaglici. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let me show you a map that we looked at last night, and this is so the Judges can understand the place that you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the Witness can be shown Prosecutor Exhibit 8A/1. You can place it in front of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, Witness, do you see Jaglici marked on that? Can you move it so -- do you recall that we spoke about this last night, and I said I would mark on "Jaglici," where you knew the village was? Do you recall you couldn't read the very small print?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you see where "Jaglici" is written on the map?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, Mr. Cayley has given you some instructions. You do not need to look for the smaller lettering but for larger letters.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Witness, do you see where "Jaglici" is written on the map? It's all right, Witness. We won't use this map. It's all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, what I suggest you do, because I realise it's actually quite difficult to orient yourselves, is if you look at Prosecutor Exhibit 1/E/1, a number of places that the witness is speaking about you will be able to see quite easily. They're already actually marked on map. Many of the smaller hamlets and hills that he mentions are marked, but, broadly speaking, you will be able to follow on this map, on 1/E/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, Witness, do you recall how many men gathered at Jaglici?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You don't need to give it to the witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: At Jaglici there were many people. I couldn't tell you how many, but there was a huge crowd. And from there we headed towards Buljim.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Were you armed at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: I had my hunting rifle with me, the one that I was given in 1968, because I was a member of a hunting club in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So it was a hunting weapon. You used it for hunting foxes and rabbits and that kind of thing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What happened to that gun?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: When we were about to leave Jaglici, my brother-in-law was with me, and we had food in my backpack, and we agreed, "Well, I'll take the rifle, and you take the backpack." So he took the rifle, and I took the backpack. That was the last time we saw each other. As of then, every trace of him and the rifle has been lost.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you said that you set out from Jaglici to Buljim. Now, you've also said that there was a very large group of people. Whereabouts were you located --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Whereabouts were you located in that group of people that was moving towards Buljim? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: I was somewhere in the middle when we reached that macadam road below Buljim. We passed their line and came down to that macadam road, and the end of the first column was standing. Somebody behind me asked, "What are we waiting for?" Some 70 metres in front of me, somebody said, "Well, we've lost the track of the column." Somebody up there swore, said, "I'll tell you where the column is," and he came down to the macadam road, except that on the left side of the hill he shouted, "What are we waiting for?" and swore again. And the fire started and shelling from that direction, and people began to scatter in all directions. Most people started to the left, beyond the stream, and I started downstream with that small group of my neighbours. So when the morning came, we were slightly above Kamenica when they pushed us downwards to Lolici. I didn't know it was Lolici until I was told that by the man who had come out together with me from the warehouse. I asked him, "Where are we?" He said, "Up in Lolici." And as we were sitting there at Lolici, they --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Witness, I just have a couple more questions for you and then we can go back to Lolici. Where did the women and children go in Srebrenica? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: We came together -- we were together until Ravna Njiva, men, civilians, women, children, all people. They were all heading to Potocari, naturally, to UNPROFOR, and we headed for Jaglici, through the woods. That is where we parted with our wives, daughters, sisters.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you said to the Judges that, I think, two ambushes took place. Who mounted those ambushes against the column that were moving through the woods? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Who else could it be but Serbs? Their troops, seeing that they fired and shelled and killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let me now take you back to what you stated earlier. You mentioned that you then got to a place called Lolici. If you could tell the Judges what happened to you at that point. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: When we got there, when we were driven down to Lolici, I said already that two soldiers were standing there. They searched us, looking for money. They tied our hands behind our necks. We crossed the asphalt and sat in a meadow across the asphalt. There was a tank to the right-hand side and one to the left-hand side. The one that was on the left did not react in any way against us, but the one -- the one that was on the other side, three times turned his gun on the group that was sitting there. There was one in civilian uniform. He had no patches. He said, "Well, lift it up. Don't be a fool." He didn't open fire on us. They brought a cistern which sprinkled us with water. Children of about 15 or 16 brought drinking water. I was sitting near the top of that group that was there. In front of me, there was a teacher sitting in front of me, and that male nurse. I heard them whispering, saying, "There must be some 2.000 here." I didn't even try to count, nor did it ever occur to me. I mostly kept my head down close to the ground, because all I would think about was my fate, what would happen to me. One asked for water. He was perhaps three rows lower than I was. A boy brought a canister, perhaps five litres of water, and he brought this water and said, "Well, some were having a go at it twice." The man answered, "Well, I haven't had a single sip." So a soldier then kicked him in the head and another one hit him from the other side, and he bled at the mouth and the nose. One picked him by the scruff of his neck and another one by his feet and took him away, some five or six metres away, and opened a whole burst of fire at him, and then I realised we were done for. He remained there, dead. Then I recognised a policeman who --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Witness, if you could stop at that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think if you wish, this might be a point in time at which to stop, because then the witness then comes on to another area that will take a considerable amount of time to explain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Cayley. We agree. Witness J, we shall now adjourn, and you will be able to pass a quiet weekend in The Hague. We shall resume on Monday at 9.30. So have a nice weekend. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
